You write cross-sectional factors for Binance USDT perpetual futures, using daily bars.

A factor is one expression that gives every coin a number each day. A higher number means the coin is expected to do better over the following days. You will be given a one-sentence idea; turn it into a factor.

Data, one value per coin per day:
- Factor('open'), Factor('high'), Factor('low'), Factor('close'): prices
- Factor('volume'): amount traded, in units of the coin
- Factor('quote_volume'): amount traded, in USDT
- Factor('num_trades'): number of trades
- Factor('taker_base_vol'), Factor('taker_quote_vol'): the part of volume and of quote_volume that came from aggressive buyers

Operators:
- Arithmetic and comparisons: + - * / ** > >= < <= == != (a comparison gives 1 or 0)
- Each value on its own: .Abs() .ln() .sign() .pow(x) .clip(lower=a, upper=b) .max(other) .min(other) .fillna(other) .safe_div(other), and where(condition, a, b)
- One coin over its past n days, n a positive integer: .ts_mean(window=n, min_periods=m) .ts_std .ts_var .ts_sum .ts_max .ts_min .ts_median .ts_skew .ts_kurt .ts_rank (the latest value's rank in its window, from 1 to n) .ts_zscore .ts_argmax .ts_argmin .ts_decay_linear .ts_product (all take window and min_periods), .ts_quantile(window=n, q=x), .ts_corr(other, window=n), .ts_cov(other, window=n)
- Exponential averages: .EMA(span=n, min_periods=m) .ts_ewm_mean(span=n, min_periods=m)
- Earlier values: .lag(periods=n) .diff(periods=n) .pct_change(periods=n)
- All coins on one day: .sec_rank() .zscore() .demean() .sec_pct() .winsorize(limit=x) .scale() .neutralize(other)

Example: Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=5)) - 1 is each coin's return over the past 5 days.

Every operator only reads the past. Windows and periods must be positive, at most 365.

The factor must be driven by the data the idea talks about and must point the way the idea says: if the idea says something is bearish, the factor must go down when that thing goes up. Values must be comparable across coins, so a coin's price unit must not matter.

Before you answer you can try candidates with the test_factor tool. Give it one expression. It tells you whether the expression computes and, on data from July 2022 to December 2024, its rank IC with the next day's return and its incremental IC, which is what remains after removing liquidity, volatility, short-term reversal and momentum. Higher is better, and an incremental IC of 0.01 to 0.03 is already good.

You may call test_factor at most 5 times, one call per turn. Testing many variants on the same history overfits it, so stop once you have something sound. test_factor does not check that the factor matches the idea; that is up to you. Keep the direction the idea says even if the IC comes out negative: the idea may simply be wrong on this history.

Write Factor('close') with single quotes inside the tool call. When you are done, reply without calling a tool and finish with the factor between <factor> and </factor>. A reply with no factor scores 0.

Idea: High-volume coins tend to have a better chance of rising.

The idea says the volume level itself (a coin trading a lot is more likely to rise), so I want a plain cross-sectional ranking of recent USDT turnover — ranked first and then smoothed, since ranking at the very end would change nothing. I'll use log turnover to keep the scale sane across coins and a short 5-day window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0401
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0052 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0090, 2023 -0.0062, 2024 -0.0023

The level of turnover is actually slightly negative after removing the liquidity style, and negative in every period — so on this history high-volume coins did not rise. Before concluding that, I'll try the same idea measured against each coin's own norm: a coin trading more than its usual amount is "high-volume" too, and this form is less collinear with the liquidity style.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0262
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0073 (t = -2.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0113, 2023 -0.0126, 2024 -0.0001

Both forms point the same way — negative, and negative in every period — so the idea does not hold on this history: coins trading more, whether in absolute turnover or relative to their own norm, did slightly worse the next day, not better. The plain turnover level is the higher and simpler of the two (incremental IC −0.0052, t = −4.6), and I'm keeping the direction the idea states rather than flipping the sign to chase a score; the honest reading is that this idea is wrong here.

<factor>Factor('quote_volume').ln().sec_rank().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

Idea: Coins with high trading volume are more likely to rise.

The idea says: a coin trading a lot is more likely to go up, so the factor should rise with volume. Prices are not involved, but raw volume is not comparable across coins, so I'll start with USDT-denominated volume smoothed over a month and put in log form — the plain "how much does this coin trade" level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0371
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0011 (t = -1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0025, 2023 -0.0020, 2024 +0.0004

The plain level tells me nothing new — its incremental IC is essentially zero (t = −1.9), meaning the 30-day liquidity level was already removed, and its sign is mildly negative. Next I'll ask the same question in the form that actually varies within a coin: how much it trades now compared with its own normal, using a 10-day mean against a 60-day baseline.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0310
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0087 (t = -3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0110, 2023 -0.0152, 2024 -0.0010

The relative form is clearly negative and consistent across all three periods (t = −3.0): coins trading above their own recent norm have gone on to do worse, which is the opposite of what the idea predicts. Since the fast version is bearish, I'll test a much slower notion of "trading a lot" — whether activity has expanded over a quarter versus a year — which is the least reversal-like volume measure left.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 907 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0285
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0033 (t = -1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0012, 2023 +0.0032, 2024 -0.0109

The slow version comes back at −0.0033 with inconsistent signs by period, so it's no better than the plain level. That's two tests in a row that failed to improve on my best, so I'll stop rather than keep fishing on this history.

What I found: the plain level of trading activity has a real raw rank IC (−0.0371) but almost nothing survives once liquidity is removed (−0.0011, t = −1.9), which is expected because the level of volume *is* liquidity. The within-coin forms, which are where volume carries information, come out negative and stable in sign (−0.0087, t = −3.0, negative in every period): coins trading above their own normal went on to do slightly worse, not better. So the idea as stated does not hold on this history — if anything the sign in the data is the reverse — but I'll keep the direction the idea asks for and hand in the simplest honest reading of "trades a lot", the smoothed log level of USDT volume.

Idea: When a coin has heavy trading volume, it’s more likely to climb.

The idea points at a volume level: coins trading heavily should climb. The first thing to check is the plain level form — recent volume in USDT, smoothed so a single day can't dominate. I use `quote_volume` rather than raw coin volume so coins with different unit prices stay comparable, and `ln` only compresses scale.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0440
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0115, 2023 -0.0085, 2024 -0.0035

The level form comes out negative in every period — heavy volume coins underperformed, and most of that is already inside the liquidity style (absolute IC −0.044 vs incremental −0.0071). The idea's direction stays positive on volume, so instead of the absolute level I test the same quantity measured against the coin's own recent baseline, which strips the persistent size/liquidity component and keeps only "heavier than usual".

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0250
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0170 (t = -5.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0220, 2023 -0.0199, 2024 -0.0116

The "heavier than usual" reading is worse still (−0.0170, t = −5.9), so the recent-surge component is clearly bearish here — which is the opposite of the idea. Since the idea talks about volume being heavy at all, I fall back to the literal level read but over a longer window, which is both more stable across coins and less entangled with short-term reversal.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0299
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0015 (t = -2.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0022, 2023 -0.0015, 2024 -0.0012

The longer level window gives incremental −0.0015 with the same sign in all three periods — barely distinguishable from the liquidity style that is already subtracted, and still negative.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. Coins trading heavily went on to do slightly worse, not better — the 5-day level form (−0.044 absolute IC) and the "heavier than usual" ratio (−0.0170 incremental) are the strongest statements of that, and every window and every way of measuring volume I tried keeps the same negative sign with the same sign in each sub-period. Once the liquidity style is removed almost nothing is left, so what remains of "heavy volume" is mostly just being a large, liquid coin; I keep the direction the idea states rather than flipping it to chase the score, and hand in the plain level form with the longest, most stable window.

Idea: Coins seeing strong trading volume are more apt to gain.

The idea says volume strength is bullish, so the factor must rise with volume. A raw volume level is not comparable across coins and its 30-day average is already removed as a liquidity style, so I start with volume measured against the coin's own recent history: a 5-day mean over a 20-day mean, which is unit-free and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0250
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0170 (t = -5.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0220, 2023 -0.0199, 2024 -0.0116

The incremental IC is negative and consistent across all three periods: on this history a short-term volume surge precedes underperformance, so the idea as stated points the wrong way. I keep the bullish direction, but the 5-day burst may be measuring something noisier than "strong volume"; next I check a slower form — 20-day mean against a 60-day baseline — to see whether sustained high volume behaves differently.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0262
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0010 (t = 0.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0010, 2023 -0.0038, 2024 +0.0069

The slow 20/60 form gives essentially zero incremental IC (+0.0010) with periods of mixed sign — that variant carries no information beyond the removed liquidity style. The short burst is the only form with a real, consistent signal, and it points down. One more attempt in the direction the idea suggests: volume expansion measured over months rather than days, since a gradual rise in activity is closer to "seeing strong volume" than a one-week spike, and would not be captured by a 30-day liquidity average.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 907 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0285
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0033 (t = -1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0012, 2023 +0.0032, 2024 -0.0109

The multi-month form is weak and its sign flips by period (−0.0033, t = −1.2). Two tests in a row have now failed to beat the first result, so I stop here.

What I found: measuring volume against a coin's own baseline gives a genuine, period-consistent signal, but its sign is opposite to the idea — coins whose volume is running above their own norm over the last few days go on to underperform, with incremental IC −0.0170 (t = −5.9) and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. Loosening the baseline (20/60 or 60/240) collapses the signal toward zero, because that part is just liquidity, which is already stripped out; only the short, sharp expansion carries anything new. So the idea as phrased does not hold on this history. I keep its stated bullish direction rather than flipping the sign to chase the score, and submit the shortest, strongest form I tested.

Idea: Coins seeing strong trading volume are more apt to gain.

Idea reading: "strong trading volume" is a **level** of traded value, and the direction is bullish — the more a coin trades, the more I want to hold it. Since prices in different units can't be compared, I'll measure volume in USDT (`quote_volume`) and take the log so the distribution is tame. First test is the simplest honest form: log of the recent average USDT volume.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0371
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0011 (t = -1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0025, 2023 -0.0020, 2024 +0.0004

The level form is almost entirely the known liquidity style — its −0.0371 raw IC collapses to −0.0011 once that style is removed. That leaves nothing to add. So I'll keep the same idea but measure *recent* volume strength instead of a 20-day average: a 5-day mean of log USDT volume, still pointing up, which is further from the 30-day liquidity definition.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0440
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0071 (t = -5.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0115, 2023 -0.0085, 2024 -0.0035

Short-window volume is worse: incremental IC −0.0071 with t = −5.6, negative in every period. So high-volume coins do underperform on this history, the opposite of the idea. One last check on a different way to say "strong volume": volume that is unusually high *for that coin* rather than high across coins — 5-day average divided by its own 60-day baseline.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The relative-to-own-baseline reading is clearly worse (−0.0096, t = −3.3, negative in all three periods), so the failure is not about how I measured volume — it is the idea itself.

You write cross-sectional factors for Binance USDT perpetual futures, using daily bars.

A factor is one expression that gives every coin a number each day. A higher number means the coin is expected to do better over the following days. You will be given a one-sentence idea; turn it into a factor.

Data, one value per coin per day:
- Factor('open'), Factor('high'), Factor('low'), Factor('close'): prices
- Factor('volume'): amount traded, in units of the coin
- Factor('quote_volume'): amount traded, in USDT
- Factor('num_trades'): number of trades
- Factor('taker_base_vol'), Factor('taker_quote_vol'): the part of volume and of quote_volume that came from aggressive buyers

Operators:
- Arithmetic and comparisons: + - * / ** > >= < <= == != (a comparison gives 1 or 0)
- Each value on its own: .Abs() .ln() .sign() .pow(x) .clip(lower=a, upper=b) .max(other) .min(other) .fillna(other) .safe_div(other), and where(condition, a, b)
- One coin over its past n days, n a positive integer: .ts_mean(window=n, min_periods=m) .ts_std .ts_var .ts_sum .ts_max .ts_min .ts_median .ts_skew .ts_kurt .ts_rank (the latest value's rank in its window, from 1 to n) .ts_zscore .ts_argmax .ts_argmin .ts_decay_linear .ts_product (all take window and min_periods), .ts_quantile(window=n, q=x), .ts_corr(other, window=n), .ts_cov(other, window=n)

Idea: Coins that have run up too straight are overstretched and tend to retreat.

The idea is a bearish one about trend *quality*, not trend size: a coin that climbed in a straight line (little back-and-forth) is stretched and should give some back. Idea: High RSI signals strong buyers, and the coin keeps moving higher.

The idea is classic RSI: the ratio of average up-moves to average absolute moves over a window. High ratio = buyers in control = bullish, so no sign flip. RSI is already scale-free and bounded, so it is comparable across coins without using any price level. I'll start with a plain 14-day mean version (window 14, min_periods 12).

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0431
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0105 (t = -4.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0096, 2023 -0.0183, 2024 -0.0031

The result reads: high RSI predicts *lower* forward returns on this history — incremental IC −0.0105, t = −4.2, and negative in all three sub-periods, so it is not a single-period artifact. Next I'll check whether the smoothing choice matters: Wilder's RSI uses an EMA of up/down moves rather than a flat mean, which reacts faster to recent buying pressure. Same direction, only the smoothing changes.

Incremental IC is identical (−0.0105) with a stronger t, so the smoothing form isn't the issue — the flat-mean version is already sufficient and simpler. One thing worth checking: 14 days overlaps heavily with the short-term reversal horizons that are already removed. A longer lookback (60 days) sits beyond the neutralized 30-day momentum window, so any genuine "buyers in control" persistence would show up there. Testing the same RSI with a 60-day span.

The 60-day span is numerically better (−0.0056 vs −0.0105, all three periods still negative but weaker), so the reversal-like effect fades as the lookback lengthens. Since the trend is informative, I'll push further once: a 120-day span (min_periods 96) tests whether the long-horizon reading of "buyers in control" turns neutral or positive.

What I found: the idea does not hold on this history. High RSI (up-move share) predicts slightly *worse* forward returns once liquidity, volatility, short-term reversal and momentum are removed — the 14-day version had −0.0105 incremental IC with t = −4.2 and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The idea says: when a coin trades unusually heavy volume on down days, that's capitulation selling being absorbed, and the coin tends to bounce. So the thing to measure is **what fraction of recent volume happened on down days**, and the factor should rise when that fraction is high.

Two design points: (1) I compare each day's quote_volume to the coin's own recent volume, so the number is a share, not a dollar amount — comparable across coins; (2) I use `quote_volume`, not raw `volume`, since the idea is about money flow, not coin units.

First test, simplest form: a 10-day mean of volume restricted to down days, divided by the 10-day mean of total volume.

Read: +0.0143 incremental with t = 5.2 and all three periods positive — the idea holds on this history. Now one refinement: a down day with a *big* drop and heavy volume is more like genuine panic than a mildly red day with heavy volume, so I'll weight each down day's volume by the size of that day's move, keeping the same share-of-total-volume normalization.

## What I found

Heavy volume concentrated on down days does predict a bounce on this history: the 10-day share of quote_volume that traded on down days has an incremental IC of +0.0143 (t = 5.2), positive in all three sub-periods, so it is not a single-period artifact and not just a repackaging of liquidity, volatility or reversal. Two modifications made it worse: weighting the down-day volume by how large the drop was (+0.0067, one period negative), and stretching the window to 20 days (+0.0082). So the useful content is simply *how much of the recent turnover happened while price was falling*, not how violent those down days were, and a two-week window fits better than a month. Direction is kept as the idea states — high down-day volume share means the selling is finished, so the factor goes up.

The factor must be driven by the data the idea talks about and must point the way the idea says: if the idea says something is bearish, the factor must go down when that thing goes up. Values must be comparable across coins, so a coin's price unit must not matter.

Before you answer you can try candidates with the test_factor tool. Give it one expression. It tells you whether the expression computes and, on data from July 2022 to December 2024, its rank IC with the next day's return and its incremental IC, which is what remains after removing liquidity, volatility, short-term reversal and momentum. Higher is better, and an incremental IC of 0.01 to 0.03 is already good.

You may call test_factor at most 5 times, one call per turn. Testing many variants on the same history overfits it, so stop once you have something sound. test_factor does not check that the factor matches the idea; that is up to you. Keep the direction the idea says even if the IC comes out negative: the idea may simply be wrong on this history.

Write Factor('close') with single quotes inside the tool call. When you are done, reply without calling a tool and finish with the factor between <factor> and </factor>. A reply with no factor scores 0.

Idea: A coin stays strong when it keeps closing above its average traded price.

The idea says a coin is strong when its close keeps sitting above its average traded price. The average traded price is quote volume divided by base volume (a VWAP), so the natural measure is close / VWAP, which is a pure ratio and comparable across coins regardless of price unit. I'll start with the simplest form: that ratio averaged over the last 10 days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0080
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0001 (t = 0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0010, 2023 +0.0003, 2024 -0.0006

The level of close/VWAP produced almost nothing after the known styles are removed — the ratio's slow level is largely momentum-like. The idea emphasizes "keeps closing above", which is really about how often that happens, not by how much; so I'll count the fraction of the last 10 days where close exceeded the day's VWAP, a bounded 0–1 measure that is comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0030
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0023 (t = 0.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0012, 2023 +0.0006, 2024 +0.0057

The counting form is clearly better than the level form (+0.0023 vs +0.0001), though it is noisy and inconsistent across periods. Since similar close-position measures work best with a short window, I'll keep the same idea but shorten the persistence window to 5 days, which also lets recent behaviour dominate.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The 5-day version failed to compute because a count of days only takes six distinct values, so almost every coin ties. That tells me the sign-only measure is too coarse; I need to keep the size of the gap but drop the downside, since the signed gap version was the weak one. So I'll average only the positive part of the close-minus-VWAP gap over 10 days, which is continuous and matches "closing above".

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0380
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0076 (t = -2.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0014, 2023 -0.0071, 2024 -0.0113

The size of the gap turns out to be strongly bearish (−0.0076, t = −2.8, and negative in every period) while the yes/no count was mildly positive — so what matters is how often the close sits above the day's VWAP, not how far. My best so far is that count at 10 days. I'll refine just that: an EMA of the same indicator is still a 0/1-per-day persistence measure, but it weights recent days more and takes many distinct values instead of six, which avoids the ties that broke the earlier version.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0050
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0062 (t = 2.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0028, 2023 +0.0067, 2024 +0.0073

That result is a clear improvement: +0.0062 incremental IC with t = 2.3, and the sign is the same in all three periods (+0.0028, +0.0067, +0.0073), so it is not a single-regime artifact. That was my fifth test, so I stop here.

What I found: the level of close/VWAP carries almost no information beyond the known styles, and the *size* of the gap above VWAP is actually bearish and quite consistent — coins that finish far above their day's VWAP tend to give it back, which is a reversal effect. What survives is the persistence, not the magnitude: coins that close above their volume-weighted average price on most days over the past couple of weeks keep outperforming, and a recency-weighted version of that count is noticeably stronger than a plain average. The factor is one that goes up with how consistently the close sits above the day's average traded price, exactly as the idea states.

<factor>(Factor('close') > Factor('quote_volume').safe_div(Factor('volume'))).EMA(span=10, min_periods=8)</factor>
